extracted.intended_audience: patent office staff, IP analysts, patent professionals, and policymakers interested in trilateral patent procedures and statistics
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and normative guidance on filing/grant procedures, patentability standards, timeline/deadline rules, and statistical metrics used across the EPO, JPO and USPTO, plus how PCT national/regional entry and patent family data are counted and interpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the Trilateral Offices will examine a filed patent application based upon novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the EPO examination is done in two phases (search then substantive examination assessing inventive step and industrial applicability). In JPO and USPTO the search and substantive examination are undertaken in one phase. International searches and international preliminary examinations by the three Offices are not included in the flow chart since granting procedure starts when entering national/regional phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Trilateral Offices, the application is to be published, at the latest, 18 months after the date of filing or priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application can be published earlier at the applicant’s request. In the USPTO, an application that has not and will not be the subject of an application filed in foreign countries does not need to be published if the applicant so requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request-for-examination deadlines and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing does not uniformly imply a request for substantive examination across Offices: filing at the USPTO is taken to imply a request for examination; filing at the EPO implies a request for search but a separate request for substantive examination must be filed (no later than six months after publication of the search report); filing at the JPO does not imply a request for examination (request may be filed up to three years after date of filing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no request for examination is filed within the prescribed period (EPO: six months after publication of the search; JPO: three years from filing), the application will be deemed withdrawn. These rules affect examination rates reported by each Office (e.g., USPTO examination rate = 100%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting of 'patents granted' (grant action definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Patents granted' corresponds to the number of grant actions (issuances or publications by the Trilateral Offices). For EPC contracting states only the EPO is considered as the granting authority when reporting Trilateral Office statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics for granted patents include direct, regional and PCT applications by year of grant. Representations are analogous to application figures but must consider that for EPC states only EPO grants are counted in Trilateral Office tallies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and maintenance fees
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent granted by an Office has a maximum term fixed by law: in all three Offices this is a twenty year term from the date of filing the application. To maintain protection the applicant must pay renewal/annual/maintenance fees; if such fees are not paid in due time the protection right expires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For European patents renewal fees are payable to the EPO from the third year after filing to maintain the application; after grant annual renewal fees are paid to national offices of each designated EPC contracting state (maintenance periods may differ by country). For Japanese patents the first three years' annual fees after registration are paid as a lump-sum; subsequent years may be paid yearly or in advance. In the U.S., maintenance fees are due at 3.5, 7.5 and 11.5 years after grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition and third-party challenge procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition systems differ: EPO has a post-grant opposition period; JPO has no opposition system; USPTO uses procedures (interference and re-examination) that are not comparable to EPO opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the EPO the period for filing opposition(s) begins after granting and lasts nine months; successful opposition can lead to revocation or maintenance in amended form. In the USPTO, interference proceedings (priority contests) and re-examination (requested by third parties or patentee) may result in cancellation of a granted patent. Opposition-related statistics (e.g., opposition rate, proportion maintained) are reported for the EPO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal process
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal can be filed against decisions taken by the Trilateral Offices; applicants can appeal decisions to reject an application or revoke a patent, opponents can appeal decisions to maintain a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: examining department first studies arguments and may revise decision; if not, case goes to a Board of Appeal which may decide or refer back. JPO specifics: appeal examiners examine supplementary reasons; if amendments to description/claims/drawings were made within 30 days from filing date of an appeal against refusal, the examiner re-examines the amendment before forwarding to appeal examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination/search workflow differences
rubrics_metrics.description: EPO separates search (with search report and initial opinion) and substantive examination ( inventive step and industrial applicability), while JPO and USPTO combine search and substantive examination in one phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a European application implies request for search but not for substantive examination (separate request required). International searches and preliminary examinations are excluded from the grant-procedure flow chart because the national/regional phase starts later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and reporting of procedural/quality metrics (rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key reported metrics include examination rate, grant/allowance rate, opposition rate, maintenance after opposition, appeal rates (on examination and on opposition). Definitions and availability differ between Offices (e.g., USPTO reports allowance rate; examination rate = 100% at USPTO because filing implies examination request).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant/allowance rates are reported as percentages of decisions (EPO grant rate 51.4% in 2007; JPO 48.9%; USPTO allowance 48.7%). Opposition rates and outcomes (e.g., % maintained after opposition) are provided where applicable. Be cautious: definitions are not always identical across Offices and this affects comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendency and pending-applications metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Pendency metrics reported include number of pending applications (at different stages), pendency time in search (months), pendency time to first office action (months), pendency time in examination (months), and pendency time in opposition (months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number of pending applications is an indicator of workload but not necessarily backlog since many pending cases await applicant action (e.g., requests for examination). Comparisons should account for procedural differences (e.g., JPO large number awaiting request for examination due to three-year allowance). Reported pendency times: example values—EPO pendency in search 19.5 months (2007), EPO pendency in examination ~45.3 months, USPTO total pendency ~32 months, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats for cross-Office comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions are not always identical in the three Offices; comparisons should be made with caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: domestic EPO filings are not equivalent to first filings because many first filings occur at national offices then subsequent filings at EPO; USPTO classification uses USPC mapped to IPC via concordance which may change scope; examination rates differ because of request-for-examination rules. The report repeatedly warns to consider procedural and definitional differences when interpreting statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification system and field-of-technology reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are classified according to the IPC which provides a hierarchical, language-independent system; USPTO applications are classified under US Patent Classification and mapped to IPC via a concordance for reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IPC does not itself define 'high technology' fields; the Trilateral Offices agree to consider specific fields as high technology (computer and automated business equipment; micro-organism and genetic engineering; aviation; communications technology; semiconductors; lasers). Shares of applications by IPC sections and high-technology categories are reported and comparisons across Offices should account for classification-stage timing differences (e.g., JPO IPC assignment completed just before the publication of the unexamined application gazette).

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT usage and national/regional entry rate metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics measure the proportion of all patent applications filed that are PCT international applications, the share of PCT applications entering national/regional phase at each Trilateral Office, and the share of PCT applications within the grant procedure at each Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications are counted in the year of filing (for PCT usage) or in the year the delay to enter national/regional phase has expired (for entry rate). EPO tends to have higher regional-entry rates due to its supranational nature; marginal yearly variations reported (e.g., EPO national/regional entry 57% in 2007). PCT-based grants are reported as percentage of patents granted (e.g., EPO ~48–49%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent families data caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent-family statistics (trilateral patent families) are based on DOCDB references to priorities in published applications and differ from office-provided application counts; publication delay means data are accurate only after several years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to priorities and flows between trilateral blocs are fairly accurate up to about 2003; numbers for newer years may be incomplete because evidence of activity in all three blocs can take years to materialize. The report notes percent of priority filings forming trilateral families varies by bloc (e.g., EPC 14.5%, U.S. 11.1%, Japan 8.0% in 2002). Detailed tables available in the web annex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting domestic vs. foreign filings and first filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic (resident) vs. foreign (non-resident) application counts and the relationship to 'first filings' differ by Office; domestic filings at an Office are not always equivalent to first filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: direct first filings at the EPO from residents of EPC contracting states are much smaller than total EPO filings by residents because many first filings occur at national offices; JPO and USPTO domestic filings are considered equivalent to the number of first filings. Users must understand these distinctions when interpreting origin shares and patent-family formation rates.
